content: Clindamycin hydrochloride has been associated with the development of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD), which has been reported with the use of nearly all antibacterial agents, including CLEOCIN HCl. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to life-threatening colitis. The use of antibacterial agents disrupts the normal flora of the colon, allowing for the overgrowth of C. difficile. This bacterium produces toxins A and B, which are key contributors to the pathogenesis of CDAD. Certain hypervirulent strains of C. difficile produce increased levels of toxins, leading to higher morbidity and mortality. These infections may be resistant to standard antimicrobial therapy and, in severe cases, may necessitate surgical intervention such as colectomy. CDAD should be considered in any patient presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use. A thorough medical history is essential, as CDAD has been reported to occur even up to two months after the administration of antibacterial agents. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotic therapy not specifically targeting C. difficile may be necessary. Management should include appropriate fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation when clinically indicated. A detailed inquiry into the patient’s history of drug sensitivities and allergies should also be conducted. Regarding its use in meningitis, clindamycin should not be employed for treatment, as it does not achieve adequate diffusion into the cerebrospinal fluid.
